title: Seek the Lord, and Ye Shall Live
sections: The Lord reveals truth through His prophets
“Seek the Lord, and ye shall live.”
The word of the Lord can satisfy spiritual hunger and thirst
Who are the “saviours … on mount Zion”?
The Lord is merciful to all who turn to Him

sayings.text: I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son
sayings.speaker: Amos, to Amaziah
sayings.why: Amaziah told Amos to go home to Judah. Amos answered that he was a herdman until “the LORD took me as I followed the flock” (Amos 7:15).

sayings.text: O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah
sayings.speaker: Amaziah, to Amos
sayings.why: Amaziah, the priest at Beth-el, wanted Amos gone. He called Beth-el “the king’s chapel” (Amos 7:13), and Amos’s warnings weren’t welcome there.

sayings.text: Seek ye me, and ye shall live
sayings.speaker: The Lord, to Israel
sayings.why: The Lord pleaded with Israel to come to Him. Going to holy places like Beth-el and Gilgal wasn’t enough (verse 5).

sayings.text: O Lord GOD, forgive, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small.
sayings.speaker: Amos, praying for Israel
sayings.why: In a vision Amos saw grasshoppers eating up the land. He begged the Lord to spare Israel, and the Lord said, “It shall not be” (Amos 7:3).

sayings.text: Who shall bring me down to the ground?
sayings.speaker: Edom, in its heart
sayings.why: Edom lived high in the rocks and felt safe. The Lord answered, “thence will I bring thee down” (Obadiah 1:4).

sayings.text: What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God
sayings.speaker: The shipmaster, to Jonah
sayings.why: The storm was about to break the ship, and Jonah was asleep below. The captain woke him up to pray, “that we perish not.”

sayings.text: Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea
sayings.speaker: Jonah, to the sailors
sayings.why: Jonah knew the storm was his fault: “for my sake this great tempest is upon you.” The sailors tried rowing to land first (verse 13).

sayings.text: Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?
sayings.speaker: The king of Nineveh
sayings.why: The king ordered everyone to fast and turn from evil. He hoped God would spare them, and He did (Jonah 3:10).

sayings.text: Doest thou well to be angry?
sayings.speaker: The Lord, to Jonah
sayings.why: Jonah was angry that the Lord spared Nineveh. The Lord answered with a question to help him think about it.

words.clue: he revealeth his ____ unto his servants the prophets
words.mean: Before the Lord acts, He tells His prophets His plans, so they can warn and teach us.
The Lord wants fairness and goodness to keep flowing all the time, like a river that never dries up.

words.clue: I will send a ____ in the land
words.mean: Without prophets, people go hungry for God’s word. The Restoration ended that hunger.

words.clue: like as corn is sifted in a ____
words.mean: Israel was scattered among the nations, but the Lord did not lose a single one of His children.

words.clue: saviours shall come up on mount ____
words.mean: When we do temple work for people who have died, we help save them, in a small way, like the Savior.

words.clue: the LORD had prepared a great ____ to swallow up Jonah
words.mean: The Lord saved Jonah’s life in the sea and gave him time to turn back to Him.
The Lord used a plant to teach Jonah that He loves all people, even Jonah’s enemies.

deep.intro: The lesson lists scriptures about why God sends prophets. In this revelation, given the day the Church was organized, the Lord tells the Church how to receive His prophet’s words.
deep.q: In D&C 21:5, how does the Lord say the Church should receive the prophet’s word?
deep.right: As if from the Lord’s own mouth
wrong: As advice they could take or leave
Only after a vote of the members
deep.why: Verse 5: “his word ye shall receive, as if from mine own mouth, in all patience and faith.” The Lord speaks through His prophet.
deep.find: as if from mine own mouth
deep.hunt: In D&C 21, how does the Lord say the Church should receive the prophet’s word?

deep.intro: The lesson asks you to read Amos 5:4, 14–15 and ponder how seeking the Lord brings life. In these two verses Amos explains what seeking Him looks like.
deep.q: In Amos 5:15, where does Amos tell the people to establish judgment, or fairness?
deep.why: Verse 15: “Hate the evil, and love the good, and establish judgment in the gate.” That’s where the poor had been turned aside from their rights (verse 12).
deep.hunt: In Amos 5, where does Amos tell the people to establish judgment, or fairness?

deep.intro: Amos spoke of people hungry for the word of the Lord. The lesson points to Enos, who felt that hunger too. Read what happened when his soul hungered.
deep.q: In Enos 1:4, how long did Enos pray?
deep.right: All day, and on into the night
wrong: For three days and three nights
deep.why: Verse 4: “all the day long did I cry unto him; yea, and when the night came I did still raise my voice.” His hunger was answered (verse 5).
deep.find: all the day long did I cry unto him
deep.hunt: In Enos 1, how long did Enos pray?

deep.intro: This week’s lesson points to President Gordon B. Hinckley’s talk about becoming saviors on Mount Zion. In it he also describes a special room found in every temple.
deep.q: In President Hinckley’s talk, what did one visitor call the celestial room?
deep.why: He says that when the Mesa Arizona Temple was opened for tours, a visitor called the celestial room God’s living room. It represents the celestial kingdom.
deep.find: described the celestial room as God’s living room

deep.intro: The lesson invites you to compare Jonah with the sons of Mosiah, who were also sent to a people known as enemies. Read how they felt about going.
deep.q: In Mosiah 28:3, why did the sons of Mosiah want to preach to the Lamanites?
deep.right: They couldn’t bear for anyone to perish
wrong: They wanted to rule over the Lamanites
Their father ordered them to go
deep.why: Verse 3: “they could not bear that any human soul should perish.” Jonah ran from Nineveh. They begged to go.
deep.find: they could not bear that any human soul should perish
deep.hunt: In Mosiah 28, why did the sons of Mosiah want to preach to the Lamanites?

deep.title: From the children’s part of the lesson
deep.intro: This week the children’s part of the lesson starts with Amos 3:7: prophets are messengers of Jesus Christ. It suggests a simple game you could play as a family.
deep.q: To help children see that prophets are the Lord’s messengers, what does the lesson suggest doing with a simple message?
deep.right: Whisper it to one child to pass on
wrong: Write it on a card and hide it
Sing it together as a song
deep.why: It suggests whispering a simple message to one child, who shares it with the others. Then you can talk about how that messenger is like a prophet.
deep.find: whisper a simple message to one of them

deep.title: From a general conference talk
deep.intro: In October 2025, Elder Matthew S. Holland of the Seventy gave a talk about Jonah, and this week’s lesson suggests it. It starts with a funny story about a girl and her teacher.
deep.q: In Elder Holland’s story, why did the teacher say a whale couldn’t swallow a person?
deep.why: The teacher said whales have small throats. The girl answered that when she got to heaven, she would ask Jonah himself.

reels.hook: The Lord tells His prophets first.
reels.seek: Before He acts, God tells His chosen messengers
reels.body: Some people in Israel told the prophets, “Prophesy not” (Amos 2:12). They didn’t want to hear warnings. Amos answered with one of the best-known verses in the Old Testament. Before the Lord does something important, He tells His prophets, so they can warn and teach His people. That’s still true. The Lord speaks through a living prophet today, so we don’t have to guess what He wants.

verse.text: Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.

question.q: What does Amos 3:7 say the Lord does before He acts?
question.right: Reveals His plans to His prophets
wrong: Sends an angel to every family
Writes His plans on the temple
question.why: “He revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.” The Lord warns and teaches His people through the prophets He calls.

bonus.q: A Liahona page about this verse explains the Hebrew word translated secret. What does it literally mean?
bonus.why: It says the Hebrew word literally means counsel, so it has to do with the Lord’s plans or intentions.

reels.hook: Called from the fields to speak for God.
reels.body: A priest named Amaziah told Amos to go home to Judah and stop prophesying at Beth-el, “the king’s chapel” (Amos 7:13). Amos said he had never trained to be a prophet. He was a herdman who also tended fig trees. But the Lord called him while he was following his flock. Prophets don’t choose themselves. The Lord calls them, and they speak His words even when it’s hard.

verse.text: I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.

question.q: What was Amos doing when the Lord called him to be a prophet?
wrong: Serving as a priest at Beth-el
question.why: “The LORD took me as I followed the flock.” Amos wasn’t a trained prophet. The Lord chose him and sent him to Israel.

bonus.q: In Amos 7:10, what did Amaziah tell King Jeroboam the land could not do?
bonus.hunt: In Amos 7, what did Amaziah tell King Jeroboam the land could not do?
wrong: Feed all of the king’s army
bonus.why: Verse 10: “the land is not able to bear all his words.” Amaziah accused Amos of plotting against the king.
bonus.find: the land is not able to bear all his words

reels.hook: Five hard times. Each one was a call to come home.
reels.seek: No food to eat, and still they didn’t come back to God
reels.body: In Amos 4, the Lord lists hard things Israel went through: hunger, drought, ruined crops, sickness and war. After each one He says the same sad words: “yet have ye not returned unto me.” He wanted their troubles to turn them back to Him. Not every hard thing comes from God. But any hard thing can be a time to turn to Him, and He is waiting.

verse.text: And I also have given you cleanness of teeth in all your cities, and want of bread in all your places: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD.

question.q: Why did the Lord let Israel go through these hard times?
question.right: So they would turn back to Him
wrong: So they would move to a new land
So they would build bigger cities
question.why: Again and again He says, “yet have ye not returned unto me.” He hoped their trials would bring them back to Him.

bonus.q: In Amos 4:12, what does the Lord tell Israel to prepare to do?
bonus.hunt: In Amos 4, what does the Lord tell Israel to prepare to do?
bonus.why: Verse 12: “prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.” They hadn’t come back to Him, so they needed to get ready to stand before Him.

reels.hook: Not a place, but a Person.
reels.seek: God tells His people to come looking for Him so they won’t die
reels.body: Israel kept going to famous worship places like Beth-el and Gilgal. But the Lord said, “seek not Beth-el” (Amos 5:5). Visiting holy places didn’t help while people took bribes and pushed the poor aside (Amos 5:12). He didn’t want them to look for a place. He wanted them to look for Him: to love good, hate evil and be fair to others (Amos 5:14–15). That’s how they would truly live.

verse.text: For thus saith the LORD unto the house of Israel, Seek ye me, and ye shall live:

question.q: What did the Lord want Israel to seek?
question.why: “Seek ye me, and ye shall live.” Going to holy places wasn’t enough. They needed to come to Him and live His way.

bonus.q: In Amos 5:8, what does Amos say the Lord made in the night sky?
bonus.hunt: In Amos 5, what does Amos say the Lord made in the night sky?
wrong: The moon and the North Star
The sun and the Milky Way
bonus.why: Verse 8: “Seek him that maketh the seven stars and Orion.” The One who made the stars is the One worth seeking.
bonus.find: maketh the seven stars and Orion

reels.body: Amos saw a strange famine coming. People would be hungry, but not for bread. They would go looking everywhere for the word of the Lord and not find it (Amos 8:12). That happened after Jesus and His Apostles died, in the Great Apostasy. For centuries there were no prophets. Then in 1820, Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ appeared to Joseph Smith, and the famine began to end.

verse.text: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:

question.q: What kind of famine did Amos say would come?
question.right: A famine of hearing God’s words
wrong: A famine of bread and water
A famine of gold and silver
question.why: “Not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD.” People would be spiritually starving.

bonus.q: This week’s Scripture Helps say Amos’s famine came true once after the prophet Malachi. How long were there no prophets in the land of Israel?
bonus.why: They say that after Malachi, more than 400 years passed with no prophets called by God ministering in the land of Israel.
bonus.find: more than 400 years passed without divinely called prophets

image.credit: The First Vision, by Del Parson

reels.hook: Shaken all over the world, but not one is lost.
reels.body: Amos ends his book with hope. A sieve is a basket with small holes for shaking dirt out of grain. The Lord would shake Israel among all nations, scattering them far from home. Yet not one good grain would be lost. He knows each of His children. He promised to bring them home again (Amos 9:14–15), and today the restored gospel is gathering them.

verse.text: For, lo, I will command, and I will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as corn is sifted in a sieve, yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth.

question.q: What does Amos 9:9 promise about the Lord’s scattered people?
question.right: Not even the smallest grain is lost
wrong: Only the biggest grains are kept
Most of the grain blows away
question.why: “Yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth.” Even when Israel was scattered, the Lord kept track of every one.

bonus.q: In Amos 9:13, who does Amos say will overtake the reaper?
bonus.hunt: In Amos 9, who does Amos say will overtake the reaper?
bonus.why: Verse 13: “the plowman shall overtake the reaper.” The land will be so fruitful that one harvest runs right into the next planting.
bonus.find: the plowman shall overtake the reaper

reels.hook: You can help save people you’ve never met.
reels.body: Obadiah’s last verse promises “saviours” on mount Zion. Jesus Christ is the Savior of all, who did for us what we could never do ourselves. But latter-day prophets teach that we become saviors in a small way when we do temple work for people who have died. We give them ordinances they need but can’t receive on their own, just as the Savior did what we couldn’t.

verse.text: And saviours shall come up on mount Zion to judge the mount of Esau; and the kingdom shall be the LORD's.

question.q: How can we become “saviours” on mount Zion today?
question.right: Doing temple work for those who died
wrong: Building a city on a high mountain
Becoming kings and rulers of nations
question.why: Latter-day prophets teach that when we do ordinances in the temple for those who have died, we become like saviors to them, in a small way.

bonus.q: This week’s Scripture Helps explain what mount Zion usually means in the Old Testament. What does it refer to?
wrong: A high mountain far away in Edom
The hills where Abraham once lived
bonus.why: They say that in the Old Testament, Mount Zion usually means Jerusalem, and especially the hill where the temple stood.
bonus.find: typically refers to Jerusalem, particularly the temple mount

image.credit: Manila Philippines Temple in the Evening, from the Church Media Library

reels.hook: Living up high didn’t make them safe.
reels.body: Edom’s people came from Esau, Jacob’s brother. They lived in cities cut into high cliffs and felt no one could reach them. They asked, “Who shall bring me down?” (Obadiah 1:3). When enemies attacked Jerusalem, Edom watched and even helped (Obadiah 1:11–14). The Lord said He would bring them down, even from a nest among the stars. Pride can make anyone feel safer than they are.

verse.text: Though thou exalt thyself as the eagle, and though thou set thy nest among the stars, thence will I bring thee down, saith the LORD.

question.q: Why did Edom feel so safe?
question.right: They lived high up in the rocks
wrong: They had the biggest army around
They had a treaty with Babylon
question.why: Their “nest among the stars” seemed out of reach. But the Lord said, “thence will I bring thee down.”

bonus.q: In Obadiah 1:5, what does Obadiah say grape gatherers would leave behind?
bonus.hunt: In Obadiah 1, what does Obadiah say grape gatherers would leave behind?
bonus.why: Verse 5: “would they not leave some grapes?” Even thieves leave something behind. But Edom would be searched out completely (verse 6).
bonus.find: would they not leave some grapes

image.credit: Bald eagle in flight. Photo: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, public domain

reels.body: The Lord told Jonah to go to Nineveh, a huge city of the Assyrians, Israel’s cruel enemies. Jonah went the other way. He took a ship toward Tarshish, probably in Spain, as far as he could get. Notice the words: he went “down to Joppa,” then “down into” the ship. Running from the Lord only takes you down. But the Lord sent a storm. He wasn’t done with Jonah.

verse.text: But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish…

question.q: Why did Jonah pay for a ship to Tarshish?
question.right: To get far from where God sent him
wrong: To buy goods to sell in Nineveh
To warn the people of Tarshish
question.why: He went “to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD.” Tarshish was the opposite direction from Nineveh.

bonus.q: In Jonah 1:5, what did the sailors throw into the sea to make the ship lighter?
bonus.hunt: In Jonah 1, what did the sailors throw into the sea to make the ship lighter?
bonus.why: Verse 5: they “cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it.” Wares are goods for selling.
bonus.find: cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea

reels.hook: Three days inside a fish, and he finally prayed.
reels.seek: Even from the deepest, darkest place, God listened to him
reels.body: Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights (Jonah 1:17). There he finally prayed. He felt thrown away, but he said, “I will look again toward thy holy temple” (Jonah 2:4). The Lord heard him. Jesus later said Jonah’s three days were a sign of His own death and Resurrection (Matthew 12:40). No place is too deep for the Lord to hear you.

verse.text: And said, I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice.

question.q: What did Jonah learn about prayer inside the fish?
question.right: God heard him even in the deep
wrong: God only hears prayers at the temple
question.why: “Out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice.” Even there, the Lord heard Jonah’s prayer.

bonus.q: This week’s Scripture Helps describe Jonah’s prayer from inside the fish. What kind of prayer is it shaped like?
bonus.why: They say his prayer is shaped like a psalm of thanksgiving and echoes many themes from the book of Psalms.
bonus.find: structured as a psalm of thanksgiving

reels.hook: The biggest and the smallest all turned to God.
reels.body: The second time the Lord called, Jonah went (Jonah 3:1–3). His warning was short: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah 3:4). Then something amazing happened. The people believed God. They fasted and wore sackcloth, rough cloth that showed sorrow. Even the king left his throne. They turned from their evil ways, and God spared the city (Jonah 3:10). No one is too far gone to change.

verse.text: So the people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them even to the least of them.

question.q: What did the people of Nineveh do when they heard Jonah’s warning?
wrong: Threw Jonah out of the city
question.why: “The people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast.” From the greatest to the least, they turned from their evil ways.

bonus.q: In Jonah 3:3, how big does it say Nineveh was?
bonus.hunt: In Jonah 3, how big does it say Nineveh was?
bonus.why: Verse 3: “Nineveh was an exceeding great city of three days’ journey.” Jonah walked only one day into it before he began to preach (verse 4).
bonus.find: exceeding great city of three days' journey

reels.hook: Sad about a plant, but not about a city full of people.
reels.body: Jonah was angry that God spared Nineveh. He sat outside the city to watch. God made a gourd, a leafy plant, grow up to shade him, and Jonah was glad. The next day the plant withered, and Jonah was angry again. So God asked: if you feel sorry for a plant, shouldn’t I care about a city of people? Sixscore thousand means 120,000. God loves all His children, even our enemies.

verse.text: And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?

question.q: What was the Lord teaching Jonah with the gourd?
question.right: People matter far more than plants
wrong: He should build a better shelter
He should leave Nineveh for good
question.why: Jonah pitied a plant he didn’t even grow. The Lord asks, “should not I spare Nineveh, that great city?” He cares about every person there.

bonus.q: In Jonah 4:8, what kind of wind did God send after the gourd withered?
bonus.hunt: In Jonah 4, what kind of wind did God send after the gourd withered?
bonus.why: Verse 8: “God prepared a vehement east wind,” and the sun beat on Jonah’s head until he fainted. Vehement means strong and fierce.
bonus.find: God prepared a vehement east wind

lines: Amos, a herdman from Tekoa, sees a message from the Lord about Israel. The Lord will roar like a lion from Zion. (verses 1–2)
The Lord will judge Syria, whose capital is Damascus, for crushing the people of Gilead. (verses 3–5)
He will judge the Philistines of Gaza and the city of Tyre for selling whole groups of captives to Edom. (verses 6–10)
Edom chased its own brother with the sword, and Ammon cruelly attacked Gilead. Fire will come on them too. (verses 11–15)

review.about: “For three transgressions … and for four” is left out of the lines; the insight card from the Old Testament Student Manual explains it.
Ammon’s crime (“ripped up the women with child of Gilead”) is summed up gently as “cruelly attacked Gilead.”

lines: Moab will be judged for burning the bones of Edom’s king. Judah will be judged for rejecting the Lord’s law. (verses 1–5)
Israel sells the poor for a pair of shoes and treats the needy cruelly, even while worshipping. (verses 6–8)
The Lord freed them from Egypt and gave them prophets and Nazarites, but they made the Nazarites drink wine and silenced the prophets. (verses 9–12)
So even the strongest and fastest in Israel won’t escape. (verses 13–16)

review.about: Verse 7’s sexual sin is folded into “treats the needy cruelly, even while worshipping” (verses 6–8); nothing about it is spelled out.

lines: The Lord chose Israel out of all the families on earth, so He holds them responsible for their sins. (verses 1–2)
Things happen for a reason, like a lion roaring over its prey. The Lord does nothing without first revealing His secret to His prophets. (verses 3–8)
Because Israel rejects the prophets and does evil, an enemy will surround the land and ruin its palaces. (verses 9–11)
Only a few will be saved, like scraps a shepherd pulls from a lion’s mouth. Altars and fine houses will fall. (verses 12–15)

review.about: “Rejects the prophets” comes from the chapter heading; in these verses the charge is violence and robbery, and the rejecting of prophets is in Amos 2:12 and 7:10–13.

lines: Wealthy women of Samaria, called cows of Bashan, crush the poor. The people offer sacrifices just to show off. (verses 1–5)
The Lord sent hunger, drought, ruined gardens and vineyards, sickness and war, but Israel still did not come back to Him. (verses 6–11)
So Israel needs to get ready to face the Lord, who made the mountains and the wind. (verses 12–13)

review.about: “Women” follows the Old Testament Student Manual (8-11), which reads the “kine of Bashan” as the women of Samaria.
Said as “get ready to face the Lord” so the line doesn’t give away the bonus answer (“prepare to meet thy God”).

lines: Amos mourns for Israel like someone at a funeral. Her armies will shrink to just a few. (verses 1–3)
The Lord says, “Seek ye me, and ye shall live.” Going to Beth-el and Gilgal won’t save them. (verses 4–9)
They hate honest people and cheat the poor. Amos pleads with them to seek good and hate evil so they may live. (verses 10–17)
The day of the Lord will be dark for them. God hates their feasts and false gods and wants justice to flow like a river. (verses 18–27)
Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, lying on ivory beds and feasting, but not caring about Israel’s troubles. (verses 1–6)
They will be the first taken captive. The Lord will give up their proud city. (verses 7–8)
Death and ruin will fill the houses. Israel has turned justice into poison and boasts of its own strength. (verses 9–13)
The Lord will raise up a nation to trouble Israel from one end of the land to the other. (verse 14)
In visions of locusts and fire, Amos begs the Lord to spare Israel, and the Lord holds back. (verses 1–6)
The Lord shows Amos a plumb line, a weighted cord builders use to check walls. It shows how far Israel has strayed. (verses 7–9)
A priest named Amaziah tells Amos to go home. Amos says the Lord called him while he was following his flock. (verses 10–15)
Amos prophesies that Israel will be carried away captive out of its land. (verses 16–17)

review.about: The KJV says “the LORD repented”; the line says “holds back,” as the Scripture Helps and the Joseph Smith Translation explain.

lines: A basket of summer fruit means Israel is ripe for its end. Its songs will turn to wailing. (verses 1–3)
People who cheat the poor with false scales and can’t wait for the Sabbath to end will be judged. (verses 4–10)
There will be a famine, not of bread, but of hearing the Lord’s words. People will search everywhere and not find them. (verses 11–14)

review.about: The lesson’s children’s part ties this famine to the Great Apostasy and says the Restoration ended it; the line stays with what the verses say, and the reel amos8-famine tells the rest.
“Ripe for its end” follows the Old Testament Student Manual (8-16): summer fruit that must be eaten before it spoils.

lines: Amos sees the Lord at the altar. No one can hide from Him, not in the deepest sea or on the highest mountain. (verses 1–6)
The Lord will sift Israel among all nations like grain in a sieve, but not one good grain will be lost. (verses 7–10)
In the last days He will rebuild David’s fallen house and gather Israel to their land, and it will grow plenty of food. (verses 11–15)
Obadiah prophesies that proud Edom, living high in the rocks, will be brought down. (verses 1–9)
Edom, Jacob’s brother nation, cheered and helped when enemies destroyed Jerusalem. What Edom did will come back on it. (verses 10–16)
But Mount Zion will be holy and a place of rescue, and Israel will get back its land. (verses 17–20)
Saviors will come up on Mount Zion, and the kingdom will be the Lord’s. (verse 21)

review.about: The line stays with what the verse says; the temple-work meaning latter-day prophets give it is in the reels and the cards.

lines: The Lord sends Jonah to warn the wicked city of Nineveh. Jonah runs the other way and takes a ship toward Tarshish. (verses 1–3)
The Lord sends a great storm. The frightened sailors pray to their gods, while Jonah sleeps below. (verses 4–6)
The sailors learn Jonah is running from the Lord. He tells them to throw him into the sea, and the storm stops. (verses 7–16)
The Lord prepares a great fish to swallow Jonah. He is inside it three days and three nights. (verse 17)
From inside the fish, Jonah prays. He was sinking into the deep, but the Lord heard him. (verses 1–6)
Jonah remembers the Lord and His holy temple and promises to keep his vows. Salvation comes from the Lord. (verses 7–9)
The Lord speaks to the fish, and it spits Jonah out onto dry land. (verse 10)
The Lord calls Jonah a second time, and this time he goes to Nineveh, a huge city. (verses 1–3)
Jonah warns that in forty days Nineveh will be overthrown. (verse 4)
Everyone, from the king down, believes God, fasts, and turns from evil. God sees it and spares the city. (verses 5–10)
Jonah is angry that the Lord showed mercy to Nineveh. He says he ran away because he knew God is gracious and merciful. (verses 1–4)
Jonah waits outside the city. God makes a plant grow to shade him, then sends a worm and a hot wind, and Jonah wants to die. (verses 5–9)
The Lord asks: if Jonah cared about a plant, shouldn’t God care about the 120,000 people of Nineveh? (verses 10–11)

insights.title: A heavy message from a shepherd
insights.text: The Bible Dictionary explains that the name Amos means burden. Amos was a shepherd from Tekoa, a small town about 12 miles south of Jerusalem, in the kingdom of Judah. Yet the Lord sent him north, to preach to the kingdom of Israel. He carried a heavy message to people who weren’t his own.

insights.title: Three sins, and four
insights.text: Amos keeps saying “For three transgressions… and for four.” The Old Testament Student Manual explains that this is a way of saying the sins were many, more than enough. It’s like our saying “a hundred and one times.” Three would already be too many, and these nations had gone even further.

insights.text: Amos first listed the sins of the nations all around Israel. Blair G. Van Dyke and D. Kelly Ogden point out that this pictures Israel surrounded on every side by wickedness. But that wasn’t the real problem. The problem was that Israel had become wicked too. Noah, Abraham and Moses were surrounded by wickedness and stayed true.

insights.title: When the lion roars
insights.text: Dr. Ryan C. Davis points out that Amos was a herdman, so he knew lions were a real danger to his animals. A lion doesn’t roar for nothing (verse 4). When it roars, you respond. Amos felt the Lord’s call the same way: “The lion hath roared, who will not fear?” He had to go, even to people who might treat him as an enemy.

source.title: Old Testament: EPISODE 47 – Amos, Obadiah – Part 1

insights.find: We hear when the lion roars, you have to respond.

paras: Amos begins his book by saying the Lord will roar from Zion (Amos 1:2). Dr. Ryan C. Davis says this sets up the whole book: picture Jehovah as a lion. In chapter 3 Amos asks, “Will a lion roar in the forest, when he hath no prey?” A lion roars for a reason. So if God is roaring, we should ask why.

Hank Smith remembers teasing a lion at a zoo as a missionary, until it roared at him from a few feet away. The sound shook his whole body. Amos’s first listeners likely knew that sound. And Amos was a herdman from Tekoa who cared for animals, so for him a lion was a real threat, not just a figure of speech.

Then come verses 7 and 8: the Lord reveals His secret to His prophets, and “The lion hath roared, who will not fear?” Dr. Davis explains that Amos felt his own calling this way: “that call for him is a roar and he has to respond to it.” As John Bytheway puts it, Amos didn’t ask to be a prophet, but when the lion roars, what do you do? You respond.

Dr. Davis adds that most of the time God reaches out to us to lift us up and help us, and our part is to respond. Amos answered by going somewhere he didn’t know, to people who might treat him as an enemy, because of his relationship with God.

And that’s how Amos feels, that he has been called by God and that call for him is a roar and he has to respond to it.

insights.title: The offering the Lord wants most
insights.text: In Amos 5, the Lord says He hates Israel’s feast days and won’t accept their offerings. Why? The Bible Dictionary explains that the offering the Lord cares about most is a righteous life. Sacrifices lose their meaning when people offer them in place of living right. What He wants is fairness and goodness flowing like a mighty river.

insights.title: A river, not a flash flood
insights.text: “Let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.” Dr. Ryan C. Davis explains that many streambeds in Israel only run for a while after a rain, then dry up. A mighty stream flows all the time. The Lord wants His people to be fair and kind like that: always, to everyone, not just when it’s easy.

source.title: Old Testament: EPISODE 47 – Amos, Obadiah – Part 2

insights.find: So God’s covenant people need to make sure that justice and righteousness are always there.

paras: In Amos 5, the Lord invites Israel to seek Him and live. Dr. Ryan C. Davis asks: how? The people kept visiting Beth-el and Gilgal, their famous places of worship, but they weren’t finding God there. For them worship had become a celebration at a sanctuary. The Lord’s answer is that a relationship with Him begins with showing justice and righteousness to the people around you.

Then he turns to verse 24, where justice and righteousness are to flow like waters and “a mighty stream.” Many riverbeds in Israel, called wadis, run only after a cloudburst and then go dry. Righteousness that shows up only when conditions are favorable is like a wadi. God wants a river that never stops.

“We’re not fair-weather disciples,” Dr. Davis says. He ties this to the Sermon on the Mount, where the Father sends rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45), and to Luke 6:36, where “be ye therefore merciful” stands where Matthew has perfect. Loving everyone, all the time, is hard, he admits, but trying makes the world better.

Borrowing Elder D. Todd Christofferson’s point that God is not a cosmic vending machine, he warns against relationships that are only a trade: you put in your money, you get your soda, and you don’t care about the machine. Jesus Christ rescued us before we could do anything to deserve it, and His disciples care about people for who they are, not for what they can give.

insights.text: Dr. Ryan C. Davis notes that the Hebrew word for saviours in this verse is the word used for Israel’s judges, like Othniel, the deliverer the Lord raised up when Israel cried to Him (Judges 3:9). The Spirit of the Lord gave them power. With the Holy Ghost, disciples of Christ help rescue others today, the living and the dead.

paras: Obadiah is only 21 verses long, and Dr. Ryan C. Davis admits there isn’t much context. The prophet’s name means servant of Jehovah, and his message is against Edom, Israel’s neighbor and relative, since Edom’s ancestor Esau was Jacob’s brother. When Jerusalem fell, Edom didn’t help. It went to see what it could get.

But Obadiah also sees deliverance on Mount Zion, where the temple stood. Where God is, Dr. Davis says, that’s where rescue happens. Then the last verse: “saviours shall come up on mount Zion.” The Hebrew word for savior here is the word the Bible uses for the deliverers in the book of Judges. In Judges 3:9, when Israel cried to the Lord, He raised up a deliverer, Othniel.

What gave those judges power was the Spirit of the Lord, which came upon them (Judges 3:10). Jesus Christ began His ministry with the Spirit upon Him, and Isaiah 61:1 describes His mission: to bind up the brokenhearted and free the captives. As disciples, Dr. Davis says, we receive the Holy Ghost to help with that same rescue.

He calls work for the dead a beautiful application of this verse, and says it is all one mission: “Our mission to rescue scattered Israel on both sides of the veil.” John Bytheway reads President Gordon B. Hinckley’s words that in the temple we become saviors on Mount Zion, and Hank Smith remembers a story President Hinckley’s father told about two boys who chose kindness over a prank.

insights.title: As far away as he could get
insights.text: Nineveh was a major city of the Assyrian Empire, more than 500 miles from Jonah’s hometown of Gath-hepher. This week’s Scripture Helps say many scholars think Tarshish was Tartessus, a city in southern Spain, in the opposite direction. Jonah wasn’t just avoiding Nineveh. He was trying to get as far as he could from where the Lord sent him.

The Old Testament Student Manual points out that they first did everything they could to save themselves another way, rowing hard for land. Only then did they cast him into the sea, praying that the Lord wouldn’t hold it against them. Afterward they feared the Lord and offered Him a sacrifice.

insights.title: Forsaking your own mercy
insights.text: “They that observe lying vanities forsake their own mercy.” Dr. Joshua Sears explains that mercy here is the Hebrew word hesed: God’s loyal, covenant love. Lying vanities are empty, worthless things. When we trust them instead of God, we walk away from the love He keeps offering us. God never breaks His side of the covenant, but we can step outside its blessings.

source.title: Old Testament: EPISODE 48 – Jonah, Micah – Part 1

insights.find: You abandon the love you could be getting and the blessings you’d be getting.

paras: Early in the episode, Dr. Joshua Sears explains a Hebrew word that runs through Jonah: hesed. President Russell M. Nelson has taught about it as the special love and mercy that come with a covenant with God, and English has no good word for it. It appears some 250 times in the Old Testament, translated a dozen different ways, so English readers often miss the connections.

Inside the fish, Jonah prays a psalm. He describes waters closing over him and weeds wrapped around his head, sinking to the bottoms of the mountains, and then the Lord bringing his life back up. Dr. Sears sees why Jesus later pointed to Jonah’s story: you are down in the depths where no one can save you, and Jehovah reaches down and brings you back up to life.

Then verse 8. Observe is the same verb as keep, as in keeping the commandments. Lying vanities translates hevel, the word behind Ecclesiastes’ “vanity of vanities”: things that go up in smoke. And mercy is hesed. People who keep empty things instead of God’s commandments forsake the covenant love He is still offering them.

“God’s never going to forsake it,” Dr. Sears says, “but we can place ourselves outside of those blessings there if we stray.” Jonah promises to pay what he has vowed. In chapter 3 the Lord repeats His call almost word for word, and John Bytheway notices that He never says, I told you so.

insights.title: A book that ends with a question
insights.text: Jonah finally admits why he ran: he knew the Lord is “a gracious God, and merciful.” Dr. Joshua Sears notes that Jonah is quoting the Lord’s own description of Himself in Exodus 34:6, and using it as a complaint. Jonah is the only book of prophecy that ends with a question. Each reader has to answer it: am I glad when God is merciful to people I don’t like?

paras: In Jonah 4:2 Jonah finally explains why he ran: he knew the Lord is “a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness.” Dr. Joshua Sears points out that Jonah is quoting Exodus 34:6, the Lord’s classic description of His own nature, and that kindness there is hesed, His covenant love. Jonah quotes the merciful half and leaves out the part about justice, because justice was what he wanted for Nineveh.

Dr. Sears notes the irony. In 2 Kings 14:25, Jonah prophesied that God would restore Israel’s borders even though Israel was wicked. Jonah was fine with undeserved mercy for his own people, but not for the Assyrians, Israel’s cruelest enemy.

Then comes the gourd. Jonah pities a plant he never planted, and the Lord asks whether He should not spare a great city with more than 120,000 people, and also much cattle. Jonah never answers. The book leaves the question with us: “Are you okay with God extending mercy to your enemies?”

The hosts compare Jonah to the elder brother in the parable of the prodigal son, and to the laborers in the vineyard who grumbled when latecomers were paid the same, from a talk by Elder Jeffrey R. Holland. Dr. Sears adds that if the natural man is an enemy to God, all of us are His enemies to some extent, “and we’re only saved through the atonement of Christ the Lord.”
