So I will light a fire in the wall of Rabbah, and it will burn up its palaces, with war cries on the day of battle and a storm on the day of the whirlwind.
And their king will go away captive, he and his princes together, says the Lord.

review.about: The refrain “For three transgressions … and for four” (verses 3–13, and 2:1–6) is a Hebrew way of saying sin on top of sin. The plain words keep the numbers, give “transgressions” as “crimes,” and “I will not turn away the punishment thereof” as “I will not take back its punishment.” No note.

The KJV’s “the inhabitant” (here and in verse 8) can also be read as the one who sits on a throne: the BSB has ‘the ruler,’ to match the one who holds the scepter. The plain words follow the KJV (“the people living in”), with no note.
A hard verse: the Ammonites ripping open pregnant women in war. The plain words say it no more plainly than the KJV.

verses: This is what the Lord says: For three crimes of Moab, and for four, I will not take back its punishment, because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime (a white powder).
So I will send a fire on Moab, and it will burn up the palaces of Kerioth. Moab will die in an uproar, with war cries and the sound of the trumpet.
I will cut off its ruler from among them and kill all its princes with him, says the Lord.

This is what the Lord says: For three crimes of Judah, and for four, I will not take back its punishment, because they have rejected the law of the Lord and have not kept His commandments. The lies their fathers followed have led them astray.
So I will send a fire on Judah, and it will burn up the palaces of Jerusalem.
This is what the Lord says: For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not take back its punishment, because they sold the righteous for silver and the poor for a pair of sandals.
They trample the heads of the poor into the dust of the earth and push the humble out of the way. A man and his father go to the same young woman, and so they dishonor my holy name.
They lie down beside every altar on clothes they took as a pledge for a loan, and in the house of their god they drink wine paid for with fines.
Yet it was I who destroyed the Amorite in front of them. He was as tall as the cedars and as strong as the oaks, but I destroyed his fruit above and his roots below.
And I brought you up out of the land of Egypt and led you forty years through the wilderness, so you could take the land of the Amorite.
I raised up some of your sons to be prophets and some of your young men to be Nazarites (men set apart to God by a vow, who drank no wine). Isn’t that true, children of Israel? says the Lord.
But you made the Nazarites drink wine, and you commanded the prophets, “Don’t prophesy.”
Look, I am weighed down under you, like a cart loaded full of sheaves of grain.
So the fast runner will not escape, the strong man will not hold on to his strength, and the mighty warrior will not save his life.
The archer will not stand his ground, the one who is quick on his feet will not get away, and the horseman will not save his life.
Even the bravest of the mighty warriors will run away naked on that day, says the Lord.

notes.text: The KJV says they “pant after the dust of the earth on the head of the poor.” The Hebrew verb can mean pant or trample; the BSB has ‘They trample on the heads of the poor.’

The KJV says “I am pressed under you,” the Lord weighed down by His people. The Hebrew word is rare, and the BSB reads it as judgment: ‘I am about to crush you in your place as with a cart full of grain.’

review.about: The KJV’s “judge” is the ruler of Moab (BSB ‘ruler’); the plain words say “ruler.”

“Go in unto the same maid”: the Hebrew says only that they “go to” the young woman, and the plain words say that, no plainer than the KJV. “Pant after” follows the Hebrew and the BSB (“trample”), with a note; Amos 8:4 uses the same verb.
The KJV’s “wine of the condemned” is wine bought with fines (BSB ‘wine obtained through fines’). “Their god” stays lowercase as in the KJV; the BSB has ‘their God.’
A few words say what Nazarites were (Numbers 6:1–3), so verse 12 makes sense.
Hard Hebrew. The plain words follow the KJV (the Lord weighed down under them), and the note gives the BSB’s reading (the Lord crushing them).

verses: Hear this word that the Lord has spoken against you, children of Israel—against the whole family I brought up out of the land of Egypt:
Of all the families of the earth, you are the only ones I have known. That is why I will punish you for all your sins.
Can two people walk together unless they have agreed to?
Does a lion roar in the forest when it has no prey? Does a young lion growl from its den if it has caught nothing?
Does a bird fall into a trap on the ground when there is no bait for it? Does a trap spring up from the ground when it has caught nothing at all?
If a trumpet is blown in a city, won’t the people be afraid? If disaster comes to a city, hasn’t the Lord done it?
Surely the Lord God will do nothing unless He reveals His secret to His servants the prophets.
The lion has roared—who will not be afraid? The Lord God has spoken—who can keep from prophesying?
Announce it to the palaces in Ashdod and to the palaces in the land of Egypt. Say, Gather on the mountains of Samaria, and see the great uproar inside her and the people oppressed there.
For they don’t know how to do what is right, says the Lord. They store up in their palaces what they took by violence and robbery.
So this is what the Lord God says: An enemy will surround the land. He will pull down your strength, and your palaces will be robbed.

This is what the Lord says: As a shepherd pulls out of a lion’s mouth only two legs or a piece of an ear, so the children of Israel who live in Samaria will be pulled out—with only the corner of a bed and the cushion of a couch.
Hear this, and testify against the house of Jacob, says the Lord God, the God of Hosts:
On the day I punish Israel for its crimes, I will also punish the altars of Beth-el. The horns of the altar (its corner points) will be cut off and fall to the ground.
I will strike down the winter house along with the summer house. The houses decorated with ivory will be destroyed, and the great houses will come to an end, says the Lord.

notes.text: Here “evil” means disaster, as the BSB reads it: ‘If calamity comes to a city.’ The Joseph Smith Translation has ‘known’ where the KJV has “done.”
The Joseph Smith Translation has ‘until’ where the KJV has “but”: the Lord God will do nothing until He reveals His secret to His servants the prophets.
The KJV says “in Damascus in a couch.” The Hebrew word is spelled almost like Damascus, and the BSB reads it as part of the couch: ‘the cushion of a couch.’

review.about: “Known” is kept: in Hebrew it means known as His own, chosen. No note.
The plain words say “disaster” for the KJV’s “evil” and translate the Hebrew (“done it”); the note gives the Joseph Smith Translation’s “known.”

A verse Latter-day Saints quote often. The plain words follow the Hebrew (‘except he has revealed’), which agrees with the Joseph Smith Translation’s “until.” No note beyond the JST, since the README’s note kinds don’t cover other cross-references.
A choice between readings: the KJV has “in Damascus in a couch”; the BSB and most modern translations read the word as part of the couch. The plain words follow the BSB, with a note. Your call.

verses: Hear this word, you cows of Bashan on the mountain of Samaria—you women who oppress the poor and crush the needy, who say to your husbands, “Bring us something to drink!”
The Lord God has sworn by His holiness: Look, the days are coming when you will be dragged away with hooks, and your descendants with fishhooks.
You will go out through the broken places in the walls, each one straight out through the gap in front of her, and you will be thrown out toward Harmon, says the Lord.
Come to Beth-el and sin! Go to Gilgal and sin even more! Bring your sacrifices every morning and your tithes every three days!
Burn bread made with yeast as a thank offering, and announce your freewill offerings so everyone will hear. For this is what you love to do, children of Israel, says the Lord God.
I gave you clean teeth in all your cities, with nothing to eat, and no bread in all your towns. Yet you did not come back to me, says the Lord.
I also held back the rain from you when there were still three months until harvest. I sent rain on one city and no rain on another. One field had rain, and the field without rain dried up.
People from two or three cities staggered to one city to drink water, but there was not enough. Yet you did not come back to me, says the Lord.
I struck you with blight and mildew. When your gardens, vineyards, fig trees, and olive trees grew, the locusts ate them. Yet you did not come back to me, says the Lord.

I sent a plague among you like the plagues of Egypt. I killed your young men with the sword and carried off your horses. I made the stink of your camps rise up into your noses. Yet you did not come back to me, says the Lord.
I overthrew some of you, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you were like a burning stick pulled out of the fire. Yet you did not come back to me, says the Lord.
So this is what I will do to you, O Israel. And because I will do this to you, prepare to meet your God, O Israel!

For look, He forms the mountains and creates the wind, and He makes known to man what his thoughts are. He turns the morning into darkness and walks on the high places of the earth. The Lord, the God of Hosts, is His name.

notes.text: The KJV says “ye shall cast them into the palace.” The Hebrew word is unclear, and the BSB reads it as a place: ‘you will be cast out toward Harmon.’
The KJV says “your tithes after three years.” The Hebrew says days, and the BSB reads ‘your tithes every three days.’

review.about: The “kine (cows) of Bashan” are the rich women of Samaria: the Hebrew is feminine. The plain words add “you women,” as the BSB does, and say “husbands” for the KJV’s “masters.”
Hard Hebrew. The KJV’s “cast them into the palace” is hard to follow, so the plain words follow the BSB (“thrown out toward Harmon,” a place no one knows today), with a note.
Verses 4–5 are scornful: the Lord mocks offerings brought while the people keep sinning. The plain words follow the Hebrew “every three days” (the Church’s footnote: HEB days), with a note.
Whose thoughts? The Hebrew says “what is his thought”; the KJV leaves it open, and the BSB reads it as God’s (‘reveals His thoughts to man’). The plain words keep it open, as the KJV does.

verses: Hear this word, house of Israel—a song of mourning that I sing over you:
Israel, pictured as a young woman, has fallen, and she will never rise again. She lies deserted on her own land, with no one to lift her up.

For this is what the Lord God says: The city that marched out with a thousand soldiers will have a hundred left, and the city that marched out with a hundred will have ten left, in the house of Israel.
For this is what the Lord says to the house of Israel: Seek me, and you will live.
But don’t seek Beth-el, don’t go into Gilgal, and don’t cross over to Beer-sheba. For Gilgal will surely be carried away captive, and Beth-el will come to nothing.
Seek the Lord, and you will live. If not, He will break out like a fire in the house of Joseph and burn it up, and there will be no one in Beth-el to put it out.
You turn justice into wormwood (a bitter plant) and throw righteousness down to the ground.

Seek Him who made the seven stars (the Pleiades) and Orion, who turns the shadow of death into morning and darkens the day into night, who calls for the waters of the sea and pours them out on the face of the earth. The Lord is His name.
He makes the weak who have been robbed strong against the mighty, so that the robbed come against the fortress.
They hate the one who corrects them at the gate (where the city’s court was held), and they despise the one who speaks honestly.

Because you trample on the poor and take a tax of grain from them, you have built houses of cut stone, but you will not live in them. You have planted lovely vineyards, but you will not drink their wine.
For I know how many your crimes are and how great your sins are. You oppress the righteous, you take bribes, and you turn the poor away from justice at the gate.
So the wise will keep quiet at such a time, because it is an evil time.
Seek good and not evil, so that you may live. Then the Lord, the God of Hosts, will be with you, just as you say He is.
Hate evil, love good, and set up justice at the gate. Maybe the Lord God of Hosts will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.

So this is what the Lord, the God of Hosts, the Lord, says: There will be wailing in all the town squares, and in all the streets people will cry, “Oh no! Oh no!” They will call the farmer to mourn, and those who are skilled at mourning to wail.
There will be wailing in all the vineyards, for I will pass through among you, says the Lord.
How terrible for you who long for the day of the Lord! What will the day of the Lord be for you? It will be darkness, not light.
It will be like a man who runs away from a lion, and a bear meets him, or who goes into his house and leans his hand on the wall, and a snake bites him.
Won’t the day of the Lord be darkness and not light—very dark, with no brightness in it?
I hate, I despise your feast days, and I take no pleasure in the smell of your solemn assemblies.
Even if you offer me burnt offerings and your grain offerings, I will not accept them, and I will not look at the peace offerings of your fattened animals.
Take the noise of your songs away from me. I will not listen to the music of your harps.
But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like a stream that never runs dry.
Did you bring me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness for forty years, house of Israel?
But you have carried the shrine of your Moloch and Chiun, your idols, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves.
So I will send you away as captives beyond Damascus, says the Lord, whose name is the God of Hosts.

notes.text: The KJV says He “strengtheneth the spoiled against the strong.” The Hebrew words are hard, and the BSB reads them as destruction: ‘He flashes destruction on the strong, so that fury comes upon the stronghold.’
In the KJV, “meat” means food. A meat offering was an offering of grain.

Stephen quotes verses 25–27 to the council in Jerusalem, about Israel turning to idols in the wilderness: “have ye offered to me slain beasts and sacrifices by the space of forty years in the wilderness?” (Acts 7:42).
The KJV’s “Moloch” translates the Hebrew ‘your king.’ The BSB reads the verse as naming two star gods: ‘You have taken along Sakkuth your king and Kaiwan your star god.’

review.about: “Seek him” is in italics in the KJV (added by the translators); the plain words keep it, so the verse reads as a sentence. The seven stars are the Pleiades, as the Church’s footnote says.
Hard Hebrew. The plain words follow the KJV (the Lord makes the robbed strong against the mighty), and the note gives the BSB’s reading.
“I will not smell in your solemn assemblies” is the smell of their offerings; the plain words say “I take no pleasure in the smell,” and keep “solemn assemblies.”
The Hebrew word behind “mighty” means ever-flowing (BSB ‘an ever-flowing stream’); the plain words say “a stream that never runs dry.”
Hard Hebrew. The plain words keep the KJV’s Moloch and Chiun, with a note. Stephen’s quotation (Acts 7:43) says “beyond Babylon” where Amos says “beyond Damascus” (verse 27); no note on that.

verses: How terrible for those who are at ease in Zion and who feel safe on the mountain of Samaria—the famous men of the first of the nations, the ones the house of Israel comes to!
Go over to Calneh and look. Go from there to Hamath the great, then go down to Gath of the Philistines. Are they better than these kingdoms? Is their land bigger than yours?
You push the day of disaster far away in your minds, yet you bring the rule of violence near.
You lie on beds of ivory and stretch out on your couches. You eat lambs from the flock and calves from the stall.
You make up songs to the sound of the harp and invent musical instruments for yourselves, like David.
You drink wine by the bowlful and rub yourselves with the finest oils, but you do not grieve over the ruin of Joseph.
So now they will be the first to go into captivity, and the feasting of those who lounge around will come to an end.
The Lord God has sworn by Himself, says the Lord, the God of Hosts: I detest the pride of Jacob, and I hate his palaces. So I will hand over the city and everything in it.
And if ten men are left in one house, they will die.

And when a man’s uncle, the one who burns the bodies, picks him up to carry the bones out of the house, he will ask someone in the back of the house, “Is anyone else with you?” He will say, “No.” Then he will say, “Hush! We must not even mention the name of the Lord.”
For look, the Lord gives the command, and He will strike the great house into pieces and the little house into splinters.
Do horses run on rocky cliffs? Does anyone plow there with oxen? Yet you have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into bitter wormwood.
You are happy about a thing that is nothing, and you say, “Didn’t we take horns (power) for ourselves by our own strength?”

But look, I will raise up a nation against you, house of Israel, says the Lord, the God of Hosts, and they will oppress you from the entrance of Hemath in the north to the river of the wilderness in the south.

notes.text: The KJV’s “a thing of nought” and “horns” are also the names of two towns, Lo-debar and Karnaim, as the BSB reads them. Lo-debar sounds like ‘nothing’ in Hebrew, and Karnaim means ‘horns,’ a picture of strength.

review.about: “Woe” is “How terrible for,” as in the approved Isaiah chapters.

A hard verse: so many dead that relatives burn the bodies, afraid even to say the Lord’s name. The Hebrew word for “uncle” can mean any close relative (BSB ‘relative’); the plain words keep the KJV’s “uncle.”

The BSB divides the Hebrew letters differently and reads ‘Does one plow the sea with oxen?’ The plain words follow the KJV (“plow there”), with no note. “Gall” and “hemlock” are given as poison and wormwood, the Hebrew words.
“In the north” and “in the south” are added to say where Hemath and the river of the wilderness are: Israel’s northern and southern borders.

verses: This is what the Lord God showed me: He was forming swarms of locusts just as the late crop was beginning to come up—the late crop after the king’s harvest had been cut.
When they had finished eating the plants of the land, I said, “O Lord God, please forgive! How can Jacob stand? He is so small.”
So the Lord turned this disaster away. “It will not happen,” said the Lord.
This is what the Lord God showed me: The Lord God was calling for fire to judge them. It burned up the great deep and began eating up the land.
Then I said, “O Lord God, please stop! How can Jacob stand? He is so small.”
So the Lord turned this disaster away too. “This will not happen either,” said the Lord God.
This is what He showed me: The Lord was standing on a wall built straight with a plumb line (a cord with a weight, used to check that a wall is straight), and He had a plumb line in His hand.
And the Lord said to me, “Amos, what do you see?” I said, “A plumb line.” Then the Lord said, “Look, I am setting a plumb line among my people Israel. I will not spare them anymore.”
“The high places of Isaac will be ruined, and the holy places of Israel will be laid waste. I will rise up against the house of Jeroboam with the sword.”
Then Amaziah the priest of Beth-el sent a message to Jeroboam king of Israel: “Amos has plotted against you right in the middle of the house of Israel. The land cannot bear all his words.”
“For this is what Amos says: ‘Jeroboam will die by the sword, and Israel will surely be carried away captive out of their own land.’”
Then Amaziah said to Amos, “Go away, you seer! Run away to the land of Judah. Earn your bread there, and do your prophesying there.”
“But never prophesy at Beth-el again, because it is the king’s holy place and the royal temple.”
Then Amos answered Amaziah, “I was not a prophet, and I was not a prophet’s son. I was a herdsman, and I took care of sycamore fig trees.”
“But the Lord took me from following the flock, and the Lord said to me, ‘Go, prophesy to my people Israel.’”
“So now hear the word of the Lord. You say, ‘Don’t prophesy against Israel, and don’t preach against the house of Isaac.’”

“So this is what the Lord says: ‘Your wife will become a harlot in the city, and your sons and your daughters will die by the sword. Your land will be divided up with a measuring line, and you will die in an unclean land. And Israel will surely be carried away captive out of its land.’”

notes.text: The Joseph Smith Translation reads: ‘And the Lord said, concerning Jacob, Jacob shall repent for this, therefore I will not utterly destroy him, saith the Lord.’
The Joseph Smith Translation reads: ‘And the Lord said, concerning Jacob, Jacob shall repent of his wickedness; therefore I will not utterly destroy him, saith the Lord God.’

review.about: Where the KJV says “The LORD repented” (verses 3 and 6), the Hebrew means He relented. The plain words say He turned the disaster away, as Jeremiah 18:8 does, and the notes give the Joseph Smith Translation, where Jacob is the one who repents.
A few words say what a plumb line is. Some scholars read the Hebrew word as ‘tin’; the plain words keep “plumb line,” as the KJV and the BSB do.
“I will not again pass by them any more” (also Amos 8:2) means He will no longer overlook their sins; the plain words say “I will not spare them anymore,” as the BSB does.
“Harlot” is kept, as in the KJV (BSB ‘prostitute’), as Isaiah 1:21 decided. The verse is Amaziah’s punishment when the city is captured.

verses: This is what the Lord God showed me: Look, a basket of summer fruit.
He said, “Amos, what do you see?” I said, “A basket of summer fruit.” Then the Lord said to me, “The end has come for my people Israel. I will not spare them anymore.”
On that day the songs of the temple will turn into wailing, says the Lord God. There will be many dead bodies everywhere. They will be thrown out in silence.
Hear this, you who trample the needy and wipe out the poor of the land,

Who say, “When will the new moon festival be over, so we can sell grain? When will the Sabbath be over, so we can sell wheat? We will make the ephah (the grain measure) small and the shekel (the price) big, and cheat with dishonest scales.”
“We will buy the poor for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals, and we will even sell the chaff along with the wheat.”
The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob: I will never forget anything they have done.
Won’t the land shake because of this, and everyone who lives in it mourn? All of it will rise up like a flood and be tossed about, and then sink down again like the flood of Egypt’s river, the Nile.
And on that day, says the Lord God, I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight.

I will turn your feasts into mourning and all your songs into songs of sorrow. I will put sackcloth (rough cloth worn for mourning) around every waist and make every head bald. I will make it like the mourning for an only son, and its end like a bitter day.
Look, the days are coming, says the Lord God, when I will send a famine on the land—not a hunger for bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of the Lord.
People will wander from sea to sea and run back and forth from the north to the east, looking for the word of the Lord, but they will not find it.
On that day the beautiful young women and the young men will faint from thirst.
Those who swear by the sin of Samaria and say, “As your god lives, Dan,” and, “As the way of Beer-sheba lives”—they will fall and never rise again.

notes.text: In Hebrew, the word for summer fruit (qayits) sounds like the word for end (qets), so the basket of summer fruit means the end has come for Israel.

review.about: A note on the play on words, like the approved one on the almond branch in Jeremiah 1:12.
The ephah (a measure for grain) and the shekel (a weight for silver) are explained in a few words: they sell short measures for too much money.
The famine of hearing the words of the Lord, which the chapter heading names. The plain words stay close to the KJV; no note, since no other scripture quotes it.
“The sin of Samaria” is probably an idol, and Dan had one of Jeroboam’s golden calves (1 Kings 12:29). The plain words don’t explain either.

verses: I saw the Lord standing beside the altar, and He said: Strike the top of the doorway so that the doorposts shake, and break them over the heads of all the people. I will kill the last of them with the sword. Not one of them who runs will get away, and not one who escapes will be saved.
Even if they dig down into hell, the place of the dead, my hand will take them from there. Even if they climb up to heaven, I will bring them down from there.

Even if they hide on the top of Carmel, I will search them out and take them from there. Even if they hide from my sight at the bottom of the sea, I will command the serpent there, and it will bite them.
Even if they go into captivity in front of their enemies, I will command the sword there, and it will kill them. I will fix my eyes on them for harm and not for good.
The Lord God of Hosts is the one who touches the land, and it melts, and everyone who lives in it mourns. All of it will rise up like a flood and sink down again like the flood of Egypt.
He builds His upper rooms in the heavens and sets the dome of the sky over the earth. He calls for the waters of the sea and pours them out on the face of the earth. The Lord is His name.
Aren’t you like the children of the Ethiopians to me, children of Israel? says the Lord. Didn’t I bring Israel up out of the land of Egypt, the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir?
Look, the eyes of the Lord God are on the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from the face of the earth. But I will not completely destroy the house of Jacob, says the Lord.
For look, I will give the command, and I will sift the house of Israel among all the nations, the way grain is shaken in a sieve. Yet not even the smallest grain will fall to the ground.
All the sinners among my people will die by the sword—those who say, “Disaster will not come near us or catch up with us.”
On that day I will raise up the tabernacle of David, the tent that has fallen. I will close up its broken places, raise up its ruins, and build it as it was in the days of old,
So that they will possess what is left of Edom and all the nations that are called by my name, says the Lord who does this.

Look, the days are coming, says the Lord, when the one plowing will catch up with the one harvesting, and the one treading grapes will catch up with the one planting seed. The mountains will drip with sweet wine, and all the hills will flow with it.

I will bring my people Israel back from captivity. They will rebuild the ruined cities and live in them. They will plant vineyards and drink their wine, and they will make gardens and eat their fruit.
I will plant them on their own land, and they will never again be pulled up out of the land I have given them, says the Lord your God.

notes.text: The KJV’s “hell” is the Hebrew word Sheol, the place of the dead, as the BSB has it.
The KJV says “yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth.” The Hebrew word can mean a kernel or a small stone, and the BSB reads ‘but not a pebble will reach the ground.’

James quotes verses 11–12 at the council in Jerusalem, about Gentiles coming into the Church: “After this I will return, and will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down” (Acts 15:16).

review.about: Hard Hebrew: the KJV’s “lintel” and “posts” are the tops of the pillars and the thresholds (BSB). The plain words stay close to the KJV.
The KJV’s “stories” are upper rooms, and its “troop” is read by the BSB as ‘His vault,’ the dome of the sky. The plain words follow the BSB there, with no note.
“Ethiopians” is kept, as the KJV spells it (Hebrew Cush; BSB ‘Cushites’).
The plain words follow the KJV (not one grain is lost); the BSB reads the opposite picture (not one pebble gets through). A note gives both.
“Heathen” is “nations”; James quotes the verse with “Gentiles” (Acts 15:17).

verses: The vision of Obadiah. This is what the Lord God says about Edom (the nation that came from Esau, Jacob’s brother): We have heard news from the Lord, and a messenger has been sent among the nations to say, “Get up! Let’s rise up against her in battle!”
Look, I have made you small among the nations. You are greatly despised.
The pride of your heart has fooled you—you who live in the cracks of the rock, whose home is high up, who say in your heart, “Who can bring me down to the ground?”
Even if you fly as high as the eagle, and even if you set your nest among the stars, I will bring you down from there, says the Lord.
If thieves came to you, if robbers came by night—oh, how you are cut off!—wouldn’t they steal only what they wanted? If grape pickers came to you, wouldn’t they leave some grapes behind?
But how Esau’s things are searched through! How his hidden treasures are hunted down!

All the men you made covenants with have pushed you out to the border. The men who were at peace with you have tricked you and beaten you. Those who eat your bread have set a trap under you, and there is no understanding in Edom.
On that day, says the Lord, won’t I destroy the wise men out of Edom and understanding out of the mountain of Esau?
Your mighty men, O Teman, will be terrified, so that everyone on the mountain of Esau will be cut off by slaughter.
Because of the violence you did to your brother Jacob, shame will cover you, and you will be cut off forever.
On the day you stood off to the side—on the day strangers carried away his wealth, and foreigners went in through his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem—you were just like one of them.

But you should not have gloated over your brother on his day of misfortune. You should not have been glad over the children of Judah on the day they were destroyed. You should not have bragged on the day of their trouble.

You should not have gone in through the gate of my people on the day of their disaster. You should not have gloated over their suffering on the day of their disaster, or grabbed their riches on the day of their disaster.
You should not have stood where the roads cross to cut off those who escaped, or handed over the survivors on the day of trouble.
For the day of the Lord is near for all the nations. As you have done, it will be done to you. What you have done will come back on your own head.
For just as you drank on my holy mountain, so all the nations will keep on drinking. They will drink and swallow it down, and they will be as if they had never been.
But on Mount Zion there will be deliverance, and it will be holy. And the house of Jacob will take possession of what is theirs.

The house of Jacob will be a fire and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau will be straw. They will set it on fire and burn it up, and there will be no one left of the house of Esau, for the Lord has spoken it.

The people of the south will take the mountain of Esau, and the people of the plain will take the land of the Philistines. They will take the fields of Ephraim and the fields of Samaria, and Benjamin will take Gilead.
The captives of this army of the children of Israel will take the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath, and the captives from Jerusalem who are in Sepharad will take the cities of the south.
And saviors will come up on Mount Zion to judge the mountain of Esau, and the kingdom will be the Lord’s.

notes.text: The KJV says “they that eat thy bread have laid a wound under thee.” The BSB reads the Hebrew word as a trap: ‘Those who eat your bread will set a trap for you.’

review.about: A few words say who Edom is: “Esau, who is Edom” (Genesis 36:1). This is why verse 10 calls Jacob his brother.
The KJV’s “his forces” is the same Hebrew word as “their substance” in verse 13, so the plain words say “his wealth,” as the BSB does. No note.

The KJV’s “in the day that he became a stranger” is, in the Hebrew, his day of misfortune (BSB), and the plain words follow the Hebrew, with no note. Verses 12–14 keep the KJV’s “thou shouldest not have”; the BSB reads them as commands (‘you should not gloat’).

“Saviours … on mount Zion”: Latter-day Saints often apply this to temple work for the dead, and the Church’s footnote points to D&C 103:9–10 and the Topical Guide’s Salvation for the Dead. There is no note, since the README’s note kinds don’t cover it. Decide if you want one.

verses: The word of the Lord came to Jonah son of Amittai. It said:
“Get up, go to Nineveh, that great city in Assyria, and cry out against it, because their wickedness has come up before me.”

But Jonah got up to run away to Tarshish (a far-off port), away from the presence of the Lord. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish. He paid the fare and went down into the ship to go with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the Lord.
But the Lord threw a great wind onto the sea, and there was such a mighty storm on the sea that the ship was about to break apart.

The sailors were afraid, and each man cried out to his own god. They threw the cargo in the ship into the sea to make it lighter. But Jonah had gone down into the bottom of the ship, and he lay there fast asleep.
So the ship’s captain came to him and said, “How can you be sleeping? Get up and call on your God! Maybe God will think about us, and we won’t die.”
Then they said to each other, “Come, let’s cast lots (like drawing straws) to find out whose fault it is that this trouble has come on us.” So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.
Then they said to him, “Please tell us, whose fault is it that this trouble has come on us? What is your work? Where do you come from? What is your country? What people are you from?”
He said to them, “I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.”
Then the men were terribly afraid and said to him, “Why have you done this?” For the men knew he was running away from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.
Then they said to him, “What should we do to you so the sea will calm down for us?” For the sea was getting rougher and rougher.
He said to them, “Pick me up and throw me into the sea, and the sea will calm down for you. For I know it is because of me that this great storm has come on you.”
Instead, the men rowed hard to get back to land, but they could not, because the sea was getting rougher and rougher against them.
So they cried out to the Lord and said, “Please, Lord, please don’t let us die for taking this man’s life, and don’t hold us guilty of innocent blood. For you, Lord, have done what pleased you.”
Then they picked Jonah up and threw him into the sea, and the sea stopped raging.
Then the men greatly feared the Lord. They offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made vows.
Now the Lord had prepared a great fish to swallow Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

notes.text: Jesus called this “the sign of the prophet Jonas” (Matthew 12:39): “as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale’s belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40).

review.about: “In Assyria” is added to say where Nineveh was. Verse 3 adds “a far-off port” for Tarshish, as Isaiah 23:1 does.
“Like drawing straws” is added to say what casting lots is.
God is spoken to here, so “you” stays lowercase, as in the approved chapters.
The Hebrew numbers this verse Jonah 2:1, and Jonah 2:1–10 as 2:2–11. The plain words follow the KJV’s numbering, one line per KJV verse.

verses: Then Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from inside the fish.
He said: I called to the Lord in my trouble, and He answered me. From the belly of hell, the place of the dead, I cried out, and you heard my voice.
You threw me into the deep, into the heart of the seas, and the current swirled around me. All your waves and breakers rolled over me.
Then I said, “I have been thrown out of your sight. Yet I will look again toward your holy temple.”
The waters closed around me until my life was nearly gone. The deep was all around me, and seaweed was wrapped around my head.
I went down to the roots of the mountains. The earth locked its bars behind me forever. Yet you brought my life up from the pit, O Lord my God.
When my life was fading away, I remembered the Lord, and my prayer came to you, into your holy temple.
Those who cling to worthless idols give up their own mercy.
But I will offer sacrifices to you with a voice of thanks. I will pay what I have vowed. Salvation comes from the Lord!
Then the Lord spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out onto the dry land.

notes.text: The KJV’s “hell” is the Hebrew word Sheol, the place of the dead, as the BSB has it.
The KJV says they “forsake their own mercy.” The Hebrew word is the one for loving-kindness, and the BSB reads it as God’s: ‘Those who cling to worthless idols forsake His loving devotion.’

review.about: Jonah’s prayer (verses 2–9) has no quote marks, like the approved poetry; verse 4 quotes what he said inside it. “Hell” is kept with “the place of the dead,” as Isaiah 14:15 does, with a note.
The KJV’s “even to the soul” means to the point of death (the Church’s footnote); the Hebrew word can mean the neck or the life. The plain words say “until my life was nearly gone.”
The plain words keep the KJV’s “their own mercy,” and the note gives the BSB’s reading.

verses: Then the word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time. It said:
“Get up, go to Nineveh, that great city, and preach to it the message I tell you.”
So Jonah got up and went to Nineveh, as the Lord had said. Now Nineveh was a very great city; it took three days to go through it.
Jonah began to go into the city, a day’s walk, and he cried out, “Forty more days, and Nineveh will be overthrown!”
And the people of Nineveh believed God. They announced a fast and put on sackcloth (rough cloth worn to show sorrow), from the greatest of them to the least.
When the news reached the king of Nineveh, he got up from his throne, took off his robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.
Then he had it announced through Nineveh: “By order of the king and his nobles: No person or animal, no herd or flock, may taste anything. They must not eat or drink water.”
“But let people and animals be covered with sackcloth, and let them cry out to God with all their might. Let every one of them turn from his evil way and from the violence in their hands.”
“Who knows? God may turn and show mercy, and turn away from His fierce anger, so that we will not die.”
When God saw what they did—that they turned from their evil way—God turned away the disaster He had said He would bring on them, and He did not do it.

notes.text: Jesus said the men of Nineveh will rise in the judgment and condemn His generation, because “they repented at the preaching of Jonas; and, behold, a greater than Jonas is here” (Matthew 12:41).
The Joseph Smith Translation has the people repent: ‘we will repent, and turn unto God, but he will turn away from us his fierce anger.’
The KJV says “God repented of the evil.” The Joseph Smith Translation says the people ‘repented; and God turned away the evil that he had said he would bring upon them.’

review.about: The KJV’s “exceeding great city” is, in the Hebrew, ‘a great city to God’ (the Church’s footnote); the plain words say “a very great city.” The three days’ journey is going through greater Nineveh with its towns around it (the footnote).

Where the KJV says God may “repent” (verses 9–10), the Hebrew means relent. The plain words say God may “show mercy” (verse 9) and “turned away the disaster” (verse 10), as Jeremiah 18:8 does; the notes give the Joseph Smith Translation, where the people repent. Your call on “show mercy.”

verses: But this displeased Jonah very much, and he was angry.

He prayed to the Lord and said, “Please, Lord, isn’t this what I said when I was still in my own country? That is why I ran away to Tarshish in the first place. For I knew that you are a gracious and merciful God, slow to anger and full of loving-kindness, and that you turn away disaster.”
“So now, Lord, please take my life from me, because it is better for me to die than to live.”
Then the Lord said, “Is it right for you to be angry?”
Then Jonah went out of the city and sat down east of it. There he made himself a shelter and sat under it in the shade, waiting to see what would happen to the city.
Then the Lord God prepared a plant and made it grow up over Jonah, to shade his head and ease his misery. And Jonah was very happy about the plant.
But when dawn came the next day, God prepared a worm, and it attacked the plant so that it dried up.
When the sun came up, God prepared a hot east wind, and the sun beat down on Jonah’s head until he grew faint. He wished he could die, and he said, “It is better for me to die than to live.”
Then God said to Jonah, “Is it right for you to be angry about the plant?” He said, “It is right for me to be angry, angry enough to die.”
Then the Lord said, “You have had pity on the plant, though you did not work for it or make it grow. It came up in a night and died in a night.”
“So shouldn’t I have pity on Nineveh, that great city, with more than 120,000 people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and many animals too?”

notes.text: The KJV says “repentest thee of the evil.” The Hebrew word means to relent, as the BSB has it: ‘One who relents from sending disaster.’
The KJV’s “gourd” is a Hebrew word found only in this chapter, a fast-growing plant, perhaps the castor bean plant. The BSB says ‘a vine.’

review.about: “Repentest thee of the evil”: the Church’s footnote gives HEB ‘relentest.’ The plain words say “you turn away disaster,” as in Jonah 3:10, with a note.
“Gourd” is “a plant,” here and in verses 7, 9 and 10 (the Church’s footnote: or castor bean plant), with a note.
“Sixscore thousand” is 120,000. “Spare” and “had pity” (verse 10) are the same Hebrew word, so the plain words say “have pity” in both.
